Created 2026-09-22 · HYPE · 922 one-sided taker surges, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29 · Source: Exp8 analysis.md, sections 64 and 68 to 71 · All reports

64. What a one-sided taker surge costs the book

A one-sided taker surge widens the HYPE spread to 1.8 times the event's own 12-hour baseline at the peak minute, and an hour after the surge ends the spread is still 6% wider than that baseline. After a liquidation cascade it is 35% wider at the same point and 19% wider two hours out. Executions do most of the work, causing 57% to 63% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge against 32% to 35% in a matched quiet window, and cancellations supply most of the rest. Counted between fills, the only grain available on every date, the surge sits 13 to 19 points above its control in each calendar period. In event time the push stands: 50 book events after an execution moved the surge-side quote, the quote sits about one further push away from the mid in every class, and it takes a median 2,824 ms to come back to where it started on a big price move against 6,032 ms in the control.

Correction: the tick numbers on this page replace the 09-21 ones

The book-event and fill-grain tick builds behind the 2026-09-21 page read the bid on every window, so on the 439 buy surges they measured the side the takers left alone. Sections 64.5, 64.6 and 64.7 are rebuilt on the consumed side. The defect, the validation and every published cell beside its corrected value are in section 68.

Setup: populations, sources and compute

Populations. The 922 one-sided taker surges, tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29, classes 561 no big price move, 314 big price move, 47 liquidation cascade. The 915 net-flow boxes, tables/redef2_imb_events_recommended_absgate.csv, appear as a comparison row in Tables 4 and 8. Matched controls are one window per event at the same clock time on the nearest qualifying day, tables/redef2_pop_control_windows.csv.

Per-market-maker rows. tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv, 118,269 (event x market maker) rows over 922 events, of which 6,173 carry an accumulation and unwind phase. The comparison file is tables/redef2_pop_event_mm.csv, 126,846 rows over 915 events, controls excluded.

Builders. code/f1r0920_reduce_existing.py, code/f1r0921_anchors_and_tilt.py, code/f1r0921_spread_phases.py, code/f1schema0922_anchors.py, code/tick0922_bookevent_build.py with code/tick0922_bookevent.sbatch, code/tick0922_fillgrain_build.py with code/tick0922_fillgrain.sbatch, code/tick0922_validate_compare.py, code/d0921_resign_skew_figures.py, code/f1r0922_tables.py, code/f1r0922_figures.py. Compute: two Slurm batch jobs on soal, 256 GB and 16 CPUs each, 4 minutes wall for the book-event tick build and 34 minutes for the fill-grain build on 2026-09-22; everything else ran inside the interactive allocation. Remaining work and its pre-run contract: plans/plan-2026-09-20-one-sided-surges-placement-skew-and-tick-population.md.

Every exhibit includes 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31. No date is excluded anywhere on this page.

64.1 Symbols and sign convention

Table 1. Symbols used on this page.

symbol meaning
t_s surge onset, the first minute of the one-sided run
t_pv flow-intensity peak, the minute of heaviest surge-side taker flow
t_c pressure peak, the minute at which cumulative in-direction net taker USD counted from t_s stops rising
t_e surge end, exclusive
t_pp price extreme, the minute of the furthest mid inside the surge
t* one market maker's own inventory peak, the minute of its extreme signed position in the accumulation direction
PRE2H, PRE6H, PRE12H the event's own 2, 6 and 12 hours before t_s, used as baselines
SAME the absorption side, whose maker fills built the position
OPP the exit side
a_pre, a_post the best quote on a side immediately before and immediately after every event at one book timestamp
Column key and source

One row is one symbol used somewhere on this page. The five run anchors and the price extreme come from the surge catalogue tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv; t* comes from the F1 population file tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv; the baselines and the SAME and OPP labels are set by code/redef2_pop_build.py; a_pre and a_post are read from ts_bookdiff_lt and ts_bookdiff_le.

Every signed quantity on this page is oriented so that the expected direction is positive. A market maker unwinding inventory is expected to bring its exit quote nearer than its absorption quote, so

tilt_bps  = d(SAME) - d(OPP)        positive = the exit quote sits nearer the touch
tilt_size = size(OPP) - size(SAME)  positive = more size rests on the exit side

Both are positive when the market maker is tilted toward getting out.1

64.2 Which minute ends the accumulation phase

The accumulation window ends at t_c, the minute at which the cumulative in-direction net taker dollars counted from t_s stop rising. Two observations recommend that minute over the flow-intensity peak t_pv: the median market maker's own inventory peak t* falls in the same minute as t_c, and so does the price extreme t_pp. Xinmeng accepted this anchor on 2026-09-21 (decision D1).

t_c is defined on the flow alone. With d = +1 on a buy surge and -1 on a sell surge, and net(u) the taker buy minus taker sell dollars in minute u,

C(t) = sum over u in [t_s, t] of d * net(u)      cumulative in-direction net taker USD
t_c  = argmax of C(t) over t in [t_s, t_e]       the minute at which C stops rising

That definition is built from the flow alone; that t* and t_pp overlap with t_c is the measurement of Table 2.

Figure 1. Where the anchors sit in a one-sided taker surge.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

Two HYPE perpetual events from the F1 one-sided catalogue, each drawn as 1-minute mid candles over the 1-minute taker flow, on a clock running from 30 minutes before t_s to 45 minutes after t_e and labeled in minutes from t_s with the UTC time beneath. A candle body runs from the minute's first mid to its last and the wick from the minute's low to its high.

The shaded band is the run [t_s, t_e]: t_s is its first minute, t_e its last, t_pv the minute of heaviest surge-side taker dollars, and t_c the minute at which the cumulative in-direction net taker dollars counted from t_s stop rising, drawn on the right axis in $m with its peak marked. t_c and t_e coincide in both events.

Taker dollars are drawn per minute in $m, surge side (buys in A, sells in B) against opposite side. The dash in each minute is the in-direction net, surge side minus opposite side, the quantity the enter threshold (3 x p95 of the pre-event net) and the stay threshold (0.25 x that p95) are compared against, with short dips below the stay threshold tolerated inside a run.

In the price panel the dotted horizontal line is p_s, the mid at t_s. The diamond marks the furthest mid searched out to t_e + 15 minutes, which fixes t_pp and the peak move M_peak in bps from p_s; the ringed circle is the mid 15 minutes after t_e, whose move gives rho_15, the share of M_peak still standing. A holds its move (rho_15 0.82; +327 bps, $38.85 to $40.12) and B reverts half of it (rho_15 0.48; -286 bps, $29.44 to $28.60). Source tables/f1schema0922_anchor_minutes.csv, built by code/f1schema0922_anchors.py.

Minutes, quantiles across events for the first six rows and across (event x market maker) rows for the last two. t_pp is the price extreme inside the surge; t* is each market maker's own inventory peak.   • The pressure peak arrives 4 minutes after the flow peak and almost never before it. t_c is at or after t_pv on 99.6% of surges, and the two fall in the same minute on 20.0% (Table 2).
  • The market maker's own inventory peak overlaps t_c. The median own peak t* lands on t_c exactly, with 55.9% at or after it, against a median 3 minutes after t_pv with 91.4% at or after it. A window that ends at t_pv closes while most market makers are still accumulating.
  • The price extreme overlaps t_c too. t_pp falls in the same minute as t_c at the median, and 7 minutes after t_pv.

Both windows run through section 64.4 as ACC_c and ACC_pv. Every later market-level exhibit on the one-sided surges ends the accumulation window at t_c. Each market maker's own phases still run off its own inventory peak t*, which section 64.3 defines.

64.3 How market makers tilt their quotes

Market makers quote 13 bps away from the exit while the position builds, then turn 1.6 bps toward it during the unwind, and the absorption quote stepping back from the touch carries the turn.

Two families of phase window run on this page, and they answer different questions. The event-level windows cut the market's own clock and carry the spread exhibits of section 64.4. The market-maker-level windows cut each (event, market maker) row on that market maker's own inventory path and carry Tables 4 and 5 below.

Table 3. The two families of accumulation and unwind window.

family window rule what it is used for
event level ACC_c [t_s, t_c) the spread, depth and taker-cost phases of section 64.4
event level ACC_pv [t_s, t_pv) the same phases on the flow-peak anchor, reported beside ACC_c
event level UNW_ev [t_c, t_e + 1 min) the phases after the pressure peak in section 64.4
market-maker level ACC [t_s, t*) Tables 4 and 5, one row per (event, market maker)
market-maker level UNW [t*, t* + 2 h) the same rows
Column key and source

t* is the market maker's own inventory peak, the minute of its extreme signed position in the accumulation direction, searched inside [t_s, t_e + 1 min). That is the rule written into the F1 population file tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv by code/redef2_pop_build.py lines 394 to 449, and it is the older section 4.4 rule. The current rule searches the peak out to t_e + 60 minutes, ends the unwind when 60% of the accumulation has been given back, caps it at 6 hours and splits it into minute buckets after t* (section 54 of analysis.md). Nothing in this section uses that rule.

One row per population and phase, over (event x market maker) rows whose market maker accumulated inventory during the event.   • While the position builds, market makers quote away from the exit, and one-sided surges push them twice as far. The accumulation tilt is -13.10 bps on the one-sided surges against -6.82 on the net-flow boxes. The absorption quote comes in 5.19 bps and the exit quote goes out 7.42 bps.
  • The tilt turns toward the exit during the unwind, carried by the absorption side. The unwind tilt is +1.55 bps with 63.2% of rows positive. The absorption quote steps 1.20 bps back from the touch while the exit quote comes 0.34 bps nearer it. Both populations agree on this to within 0.2 bps.

Resting size across the two population files (decision D3, resolved in section 65 of analysis.md). The tenfold gap in resting size between the two files of record, 651 HYPE against 64 on the shocked accumulation side, is the order-store placement-day defect, not the active-market-maker rule. Both files predate the 2026-09-15 fix, and the net-flow file writes exactly zero resting size on 30.5% of its shocked rows. With the fix and the post-only rule the medians are 764 and 469 HYPE, and on the 512 (date, wallet) pairs present in both catalogues they are 802 and 801. The remaining gap between 764 and 469 comes from which wallets each catalogue flags as shocked. The tilt in Tables 4 and 5 holds under the fix: rerun on the order-fixed files, every median shifts by at most 0.17 bps and every share of rows tilted to the exit by at most 0.9 points, on 5% more rows for the surges and 32% more for the net-flow boxes (tables/d0921_tilt_orderfix_compare.csv, code/d0921_tilt_orderfix_check.py). Section 65 recommends taking resting size from the order-fixed files (its decision D3a). It also finds that quiet market-maker-labeled wallet-days, under 50 HYPE orders or under 10 fills, are 2.3% of the kept rows and 0.07% of absorbing USD, so no flow result on this page depends on them.

64.4 Spread, depth and taker cost by phase

The spread peaks at the flow peak at 1.8 times the event's own 12-hour baseline, and after a liquidation cascade it is still 35% wider than that baseline an hour after the surge ends.

Figure 3. Quoted spread by phase.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

917 of the 922 surges have both book minutes in the panel and a 12-hour baseline. The x axis is the phase sequence: the accumulation window ACC_c, the peak minute at t_pv, then 5-minute buckets measured from the surge end t_e. Top panel: the time-weighted mean quoted spread in cents, median across events, band p25 to p75. Middle panel: the same spread divided by the same event's own PRE12H median. Bottom panel: the surge-side volume-weighted effective half-spread minus the same event's own PRE2H value. Every panel is a median across events, one event one vote. Minutes with no book row are dropped.

At the peak minute the ratio runs from 0.99 at p5 to 3.95 at p95, so a twentieth of surges show no widening at all while a twentieth more than triple.

  • The spread peaks at the flow peak, not at the surge end. It reaches 1.82 times the event's own 12-hour baseline at t_pv and is down to 1.46 in the first 5 minutes after the surge ends (Table 6).
  • An hour later the spread is 6% wider than the baseline, and after a liquidation cascade 35% wider. At 115 to 120 minutes the figures are 2% and 19%. The cascade median is above every other class at every phase (Table 7).
  • Near depth holds through the surge. Surge-side resting size within 10 bps of the mid stays at 1.01 to 1.09 times its own PRE2H level at every phase, including the peak minute, with p25 between 0.76 and 0.84 across events and p75 between 1.31 and 1.53. The surge is absorbed by a wider quoted spread while near depth holds.
  • Surge-side takers pay more while the surge runs. The effective half-spread is 5.26 bps above the event's own prior 2 hours at the peak minute, 15.10 bps for cascades, and 0.42 bps in the first 5 minutes after the end. From 5 minutes onward it runs 1.0 to 1.8 bps below that baseline.

The last point sits opposite the net-flow result in section 55 of analysis.md, which found surge-side takers paying 0.61 bps more in the first 10 minutes and 0.28 bps more at 20 to 30 minutes. The two use different baselines: section 55 compares against a matched control window on another day, this page against the event's own preceding 2 hours, which are themselves already wide. A market that is quiet by its own recent standard can still be expensive by the standard of an ordinary day.

The median spread is one tick, so the mean is the statistic

HYPE's tick is $0.001. The median quoted spread is one tick in every window, so a median comparison across phases is degenerate and the page uses the time-weighted mean in cents. The share of minutes quoted at one tick falls from 16.5% over the 12 hours before the surge to 10.0% over the 2 hours before it and to 0% at the median during and after. Both statistics are in tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_levels.csv, with p75, p90 and p95 in cents and the mean in bps.

64.5 What moves the surge-side quote

Executions cause 57% to 63% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge, against 32% to 35% in a matched quiet window, a ratio of 1.7 to 1.9. The single-episode reading in sections 28 and 30 of analysis.md, 93.5%, was measured at the same book-event grain on the same side and is a property of the most intense interval of one December 2025 episode.

Setup: the measure, the side, and why the grain matters

One tick is one book-event timestamp. The side measured is the one the takers consumed, the ask on a buy surge and the bid on a sell surge; section 68 records the build that got this wrong and what it changed. With m the ts_bookdiff_lt mid and the sign chosen so that away from the mid is positive:

c_bps = 1e4 * s * (a_post - a_pre) / m      what the events at this timestamp did
r_bps = 1e4 * s * (a_next - a_post) / m     what happened before the next book event

A tick with c > 0 is classified trade when a surge-side taker at that timestamp covered the whole a_pre level (or reached two or more levels), mixed when a taker was present but did not cover it, and cancel when no taker was present. A tick with c < 0 is a post, a quote arriving inside the previous best.

The replacement depth is the size standing at the surge-side best k book events after the pushing execution, over the size that stood on the level the execution ate:

D(k) = q(best, k book events after the push) / q(a_pre)

D(k) > 1 means the level now standing is thicker than the one that was eaten. It is a different object from the phi of section 69, which is read at the next fill and not at a fixed count of book events.

r_bps is zero by construction at this grain, because lt(t_i+1) is the same book state as le(t_i) when consecutive rows are the book events. Measured, it is non-zero on 0.03% to 0.11% of ticks and is kept only as a validation column. Replenishment here is the next post tick, not a gap between two ticks. The a_post to a_next gap carries information only when the grain is coarser than the book events, which is the fill grain of sections 64.6 and 69.

Scope. 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 only, the range where the phase tables carry a row at every book event. That is 398 of the 922 surges, 397 of the 915 boxes and 243 controls, 33.4 million tick rows. Outside the range the tables are keyed at fill microseconds, so "the next row" means something else and the two cannot be pooled; section 64.6 measures every date at fill grain instead.

64.6 The same measure between fills, on every date

Counted between consecutive fills, executions cause 76% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge and 59% in a matched quiet window, across every date. The surge sits 13.3, 18.9 and 15.4 points above its control in the three calendar periods, so the surge effect of section 64.5 holds on the 57% of events that the book-event grain cannot reach. The level depends on the grain: on the same events, counting between fills raises the execution share by 12 points on the surges and 17 on the controls.

Setup: the fill grain, and how it relates to the book-event grain

Outside 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 the phase tables hold a row only where a fill occurred. On all 244 such dates used here, every key is a taker or maker fill timestamp and no fill timestamp is missing from the table. A tick at fill grain is one fill timestamp:

c_bps = 1e4 * s * (le(t_i)   - lt(t_i)) / m     the fills and cancels at fill timestamp t_i
r_bps = 1e4 * s * (lt(t_i+1) - le(t_i)) / m     every placement and cancel before the next fill

Gross travel away from the mid is the positive part of c plus the positive part of r. The execution share is the travel from trade ticks over that total, and the between-fill share is the positive part of r over the same total. A tick is trade when the executed surge-side size at that timestamp covers the whole lt level or the taker reached two levels. Executed size is the larger of the taker size consuming that side and the maker size resting on it, because the maker and taker row sets do not balance on 2025-03-24 to 2025-05-25.

Inside the range the same code subsets the book-event rows to the fill timestamps, which gives the same object, and computes the book-event grain beside it with the same classification. At book-event grain it reproduces tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv on all 3,109 (event x side x phase) units, with a largest difference of 1.1e-16.

Why the grain moves the level. A cancel that pulls the best quote away and a placement that restores it before the next fill both count as travel at book-event grain, and they net to zero between two fills. Counting between fills removes that round trip. Gross travel falls to 0.83 of its book-event value on the surges and to 0.67 on the controls, whose quotes flicker more, so the control's execution share rises more.

Scope. 910 of the 922 surges, all 915 boxes and all 558 control windows, 75.3 million tick rows over both grains. The 12 surges without a unit are zero-length in the catalogue (t_s = t_e), so they have no surge window. Compute: one Slurm batch job on soal, 256 GB and 16 CPUs, 2026-09-22, 34 minutes wall, 17.5 GiB peak memory, code/tick0922_fillgrain_build.py with code/tick0922_fillgrain.sbatch.

Remark that needs attention. Before 2025-09-27 the fill-grain execution share is 13 to 18 points higher than inside the range, on surges, boxes and controls alike (0.838, 0.799 and 0.705 against 0.711, 0.671 and 0.522), with less travel between fills (0.109 against 0.197 on the surges). The storage format is ruled out: 2026-04-16 to 2026-06-30 is stored the same way as the early months and matches the in-range values. The incomplete early fill record is ruled out too, because the later part of the early period, 2025-05-26 to 2025-09-26, reads higher still, 0.846 on the surges against 0.819 on the incomplete dates. The candidate cause is fewer quote placements and cancels per fill in the early months. Test: count order placements and cancels per fill by month from the order store, and check that the monthly count tracks the between-fill share.

64.7 How fast the quote comes back

Every number in this section is the share of one execution's push that is no longer standing at a horizon,

R(h) = 1 - (level at h - level before the push) / push

so R = 0 leaves the push intact, R = 1 returns the quote to its pre-execution level and R < 0 means the quote traveled further out. Horizons h are counted in book events first and in clock time second.

The push stands in event time and in clock time alike: 50 book events after an execution moved the surge-side quote, the quote sits 0.83 to 1.18 further pushes away from the mid depending on the class, and 30 seconds after the execution it sits 0.94 to 1.74 further pushes out. The matched controls barely move: across their three classes the share reverted sits within 0.02 of zero at every horizon except 100 milliseconds, where it runs 0.02 to 0.11, and 20 book events and 30 seconds on the 32-event cascade class, where the quote drifts 0.13 and 0.12 further out.

Top panel counts horizons in book events, bottom panel in clock time; both axes are ordered categories drawn at equal spacing, not to scale. Each line is the median within an event, then the median across events. The control line is its no-big-move class. The big-price-move control sits within 0.03 of it at every horizon; the 32-event cascade control sits within 0.02 except at 100 milliseconds, 20 book events and 30 seconds, where it is 0.07, 0.13 and 0.12 away.

Median within an event of the time from the pushing execution until the surge-side best quote is back at or inside its pre-execution level, then quantiles across events. A push that never returns before the window ends is censored at the window end; that happens on a median 1.4% of surge pushes and 0.0% of control pushes.   • The push survives the next book event. At one book event the share reverted is 0.000 to 0.069 in every class (Table 13).
  • 50 book events later the quote has traveled further out in every class, by 1.18 pushes on a big price move, 0.94 in a liquidation cascade and 0.83 with no big move, against 0.00 in each class's own matched control.
  • At 30 seconds the same holds, 1.74, 1.32 and 0.94 further pushes out on the three surge classes, against 0.00, 0.12 and 0.00 in their own matched controls, so the event clock and the wall clock agree.
  • The quote crosses its old level sooner during a surge while drifting further from it. A push returns to its pre-execution level in a median 2,824 ms on a big-price-move surge against 6,032 ms in its matched control, while book events arrive a median 88 ms apart inside a surge window against 90 ms in a control, so the arrival rate is not what makes the surge look quicker. Gross travel away from the mid is 2,094 bps in a surge window against 1,545 bps in the control (Table 16), so the surge-side quote crosses its old level more often on the way to sitting further out.
  • Over the whole window the surge-side quote ends further from the mid than it started. Gross travel toward the mid is 0.89 to 0.91 times gross travel away from it on the surges and 1.01 in every control class, and the net move is +97 to +191 bps away from the mid on the surges against -8 to -26 bps in the controls (Table 16).
  • At fill grain, on every date, the push stands in clock time too. On big-price-move surges a median 5% of a push has reverted after 1 second inside the book-event range and 16% outside it, none of it is back at 5 seconds, and by 30 seconds the quote has traveled a further 1.71 to 1.73 pushes out (Table 15).

64.8 Where this sits in the order-book resiliency literature

Lining up on aggressive orders and tracking the spread, the best quote and the depth over the following book events is the design of Biais, Hillion and Spatt (1995) and of Degryse, de Jong, van Ravenswaaij and Wuyts (2005). Large (2007) is the hazard-model version, which estimates a replenishment intensity in place of a level path and is the natural next step once the question becomes how long resilience takes.

Three choices here follow that literature. Horizons are counted in book events first and clock time second, because the arrival rate itself changes during a surge. Prints are ranked into deciles within their own event, so the comparison is between prints of the same episode. And every number carries a matched quiet-window benchmark, because the level alone has no meaning.

64.9 The book tables

ts_bookdiff_lt is a reconstruction of the book strictly before every event at a timestamp; its best quotes match the last raw Tardis snapshot on 55% to 85% of rows, and its row grain changes by date.

What was verified, and on which days

Three phase tables exist for HYPE. ts_bookdiff_lt is the book strictly before every event at a timestamp. ts_bookdiff without a suffix is after arrivals and updates but before fills, so it is not a post-trade book. ts_bookdiff_le is after fills and then cancellations, and it is the post-trade state. On 2025-12-17, at taker-fill microseconds, lt and the middle phase agree on 87.2% of best prices while the middle phase and le differ on 65% of best-ask sizes.

The row grain changes by date. On 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 all three are keyed at every book event: 895,128 rows on 2025-12-17 against 116,988 taker-fill microseconds, and 100% of the extra timestamps are order placement or status timestamps. Outside that range they are keyed at fill microseconds only; on all 244 out-of-range dates used in section 64.6, every key is a taker or maker fill timestamp. Storage differs too, (timestamp, state_id) joined to ts_bookdiff_states inside the range and 20 inline price and amount columns outside it.

ts_bookdiff_lt was never overwritten by the forder work. The 2026-07-30 ordered walker replaced only p_mid in grouped_trade_oid and grouped_trade_oid_leverage on 201 dates; restore_legacy_pmid.py reverted it and archived the bad values as pmid_ordered_invalid_2025-09-27_2026-04-15/. Recomputing p_mid from today's lt reproduces the stored value on 100.0000% of taker rows on 2025-12-17, inside the overwrite window, and on 99.98% on 2025-04-15, and p_mid = p_0 + s * hs_component / size holds on 100% of rows on all three days tested. The forder ceiling defect is a different table: kcalc3.py's gord = tag * 10^7 + forder overflow in k_fills_by_day on 46 dates.

64.10 What this does not establish

  • The book tables are unsafe timestamp proxies. The 2026-08-03 correction demoted every ts_bookdiff* output because the builder's tie-break, arrivals then fills then terminal statuses, is not HyperCore's documented action ordering. Every tick number on this page inherits that.
  • A tick carrying a fill and a placement at the same microsecond cannot be split. The execution share in section 64.5 is therefore a lower bound on how mixed the ticks really are.
  • The book-event numbers cover 43% of each catalogue. Section 64.6 carries the surge-over-control comparison to every date at fill grain, a coarser measure whose level runs 12 to 17 points higher on the same events.
  • Every comparison is descriptive, against a matched window or against the event's own past.
  • The quote tilt records where orders sat, not where they were placed. A minute-snapshot distance moves on its own when takers consume the levels in front of a standing quote. The placement-time measure, distance to the touch at each order's own order_timestamp, does not exist yet.
  • The unwind tilt is a window average on the older market-maker phase rule. The standing rule is to split the unwind by the share of the peak excursion still held, 100-75, 75-50, 50-25 and 25-0%, because a 2-hour average hides a lean that lasts 15 minutes. That split is not built for this catalogue, and neither is the current 4.4 rule of Table 3.
  • The class ordering in section 64.5 rests on 35 cascade units and overlapping interquartile ranges.

64.11 Decisions waiting

Decisions D1, D2 and D4 were taken on 2026-09-21 and are applied on this page: t_c ends the accumulation window (section 64.2), section 50's three figures are redrawn on the expected-positive sign (section 50.8), and the fill-grain measure runs on every date (section 64.6). D4 keeps its verdict under the side correction, because the paired grain difference is 11.9 to 16.9 points and the rule asked for 5. D3, the active-market-maker reconciliation, is resolved in section 65 of analysis.md and summarized in section 64.3; its follow-on D3a, taking resting size from the order-fixed files, is listed there. D5, moving the live report onto the new sign, is approved.

68. The tick decomposition measured the wrong side on buy surges

The book-event and fill-grain tick builds behind the 2026-09-21 page read the bid on every window. A taker buy lifts the ask, so on the 439 buy surges, 386 buy boxes and 240 buy controls the published numbers describe the side the surge did not touch. Rebuilt on the consumed side, the execution share of the quote's travel rises by 2.4 to 5.3 points on the surges and falls by 1.2 to 3.5 points on the controls, so the surge sits 23 to 30 points above its matched quiet window instead of 17 to 24. The reversion reading changes sign: 50 book events after an execution the surge-side quote has traveled 1.18 further pushes out on a big price move, where the published table read the push as intact.

Setup: the defect, the fix, and what is unchanged

The defect. code/tick0920_bookevent_build.py:197 and code/tick0921_fillgrain_build.py:173 both read the window side as

side = "ask" if str(w.hit_side).lower().startswith("a") else "bid"

hit_side is buy or sell in all three catalogues, tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv, tables/redef2_imb_events_recommended_absgate.csv and tables/redef2_pop_control_windows.csv. No value starts with a, so the expression returned bid for all 2,395 windows. hit_side names the taker's direction, so the consumed side is the ask on a buy window and the bid on a sell window. The published builds therefore measured the surge side on the 1,330 sell windows and the opposite side on the 1,065 buy windows.

The fix. code/tick0922_bookevent_build.py and code/tick0922_fillgrain_build.py are copies of the two published builders with one line replaced,

side = "ask" if str(w.hit_side).lower() == "buy" else "bid"

and a check in windows() that rejects any hit_side outside {buy, sell}. The parts roots are data/tick0922_parts_book/ and data/tick0922_parts/, and the tables carry the prefixes tick0922b_ at book-event grain and tick0922_ at fill grain. The fill build's reproduction check now targets tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv, and it writes tables/tick0922_by_period.csv in the reduce, which a separate script did before. Nothing else in either builder moved.

What is unchanged. Window membership, coverage and every count: 3,109 book-grain (event x side x phase) units, 10,282 fill-build units, 915 boxes, 910 surges and 558 controls with a fill-grain surge window, 0 failed dates. The tick0920 and tick0921 code, parts and tables stay on disk untouched and remain the record of what the 09-21 page published.

Compute. Two Slurm batch jobs on soal, 256 GB and 16 CPUs, 8 workers, 2026-09-22: code/tick0922_bookevent.sbatch 4 minutes wall and 6.1 GiB peak, code/tick0922_fillgrain.sbatch 34 minutes and 17.5 GiB.

68.1 Findings

As expected.

  • Executions cause 57% to 63% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid, against 32% to 35% in a matched quiet window. The published reading was 52% to 59% against 35%, a ratio of 1.5 to 1.7; corrected it is 1.7 to 1.9 (Table 18).
  • The surge-over-control gap widens by 6 to 8 points in every class, from 16.7, 24.0 and 20.8 points to 22.9, 29.8 and 28.0 on the no-big-move, cascade and big-price-move classes.
  • The three classes still sit within 6 points of each other, 57.2% to 63.0% against 52.1% to 59.3% published, so the ordering across classes remains unestablished.
  • Net quote movement inside the surge window turns positive, +188 bps on a big-price-move surge against -70 bps published, which is what measuring the consumed side implies.
  • The fill-grain gap widens in every period, to +13.3, +18.9 and +15.4 points on the surges from +9.5, +13.5 and +9.6 published, and the boxes move the same way (Table 19).
  • The D4 decision rule keeps its verdict. The median paired difference between the two grains is 11.9, 14.2 and 16.9 points, all above the 5-point threshold, so the book-event and fill-grain measures keep separate roles exactly as section 64.6 states. The grain effect itself moves by at most 0.5 points in any population, because the cancel-and-repost round trips it removes happen on both sides of the book.
  • The top decile pushes 7.11 bps, 30% more than the published 5.47, and surge-side prints are larger than the published table showed at every decile above the first, a median 2,985 HYPE at decile 10 against 1,931, because the consumed side carries the surge's own flow.

Not as expected (possible design cause).

  • Two published reversion cells change sign. At 50 book events the big-price-move class reads -1.18 against a published 0.004 and the no-big-move class -0.83 against -0.199, and at 30 seconds -1.74 against 0.009 and -0.94 against 0.000 (Table 20). Possible design cause: the opposite side of a one-sided surge is the side nobody is consuming, so its best quote drifts back toward the mid while the consumed side is being walked outward; measuring it read a push that stood still. Check: the matched controls, where neither side is being consumed, move by at most 0.06 at any horizon, which is what the mechanism predicts.
  • Gross travel toward the mid falls below gross travel away on the surges. The ratio is 0.89 to 0.91 corrected against 0.93 to 1.05 published, so the surge-side quote does not fully recover its level inside the window; on the controls it stays at 1.01. Possible design cause: the same asymmetry, read on the level in place of the push.
  • A median 1.4% of surge pushes never return to their pre-execution level inside the window, against 0.0% published, and the median return time rises from 1,716 ms to 2,824 ms on a big-price-move surge. Possible design cause: a censored push is one the window ends on, so the share is bounded by how long a surge runs; check whether the 1.4% concentrates on the shortest surges.
  • 4 fill-build ticks classify differently, all outside the surge window. They fall on three units and move between trade and mixed, shifting share_trade by at most 0.00065 on 4 rows of 39,629,127. Possible design cause: the executed size and the resting level are equal to seven significant figures at those ticks, 2.5199999809 against 2.5200002194 HYPE on 2025-08-12, so the ex >= q_pre - 1e-9 coverage rule sits on a tie and the last bit of the float sum decides it. The published builder carries the same tie; it is not introduced here, and every EVENT-phase unit is unaffected.

68.2 Validation

Every check in tables/tick0922_validation.csv
  • On the 1,330 sell windows the new parts reproduce the published parts row for row. 17,952,428 book-event rows and 39,629,127 fill-build rows carry identical c_bps and r_bps, largest absolute difference 0, and identical kind on every book-event row and on all but 4 fill-build rows.
  • Every buy window now carries side = ask and every sell window side = bid, against bid on every window of the published parts.
  • The decomposition shares sum to 1 on all 3,109 book-grain units and all 10,282 fill-build units, largest deviation 3.3e-16.
  • At book grain with the taker-only rule the fill build reproduces tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv on all 3,109 units, largest difference 1.1e-16.
  • The 1,786 book-grain units whose side did not change carry exactly the published share_trade, and so do all 1,915 sell-window fill-build units of the EVENT phase.
  • tables/tick0922_vs_tick0921_headline.csv pairs each published median with its corrected value, the difference, and the count of buy windows in the cell, over 1,548 rows keyed by metric, grain, range group, population, class, phase, horizon and decile.

68.3 What the tick0920 and tick0921 outputs are

The published parts and tables stay on disk unchanged. They are the record of the tick exhibits in the 2026-09-21 letter report_one_sided_surges_09-21c.html. Every cell of those exhibits that rests on a buy window is superseded by the tick0922 tables. The rows of tables/tick0922_vs_tick0921_headline.csv marked range_group = "in range (book build)" compare tick0920 with tick0922b; the rest compare tick0921 with tick0922, whose own book-grain columns classify on maker-inclusive executed size and therefore read a few tenths of a point apart from the book build's, in the published run as in this one.

69. What a print consumes and what comes back before the next trade

A taker print takes the surge-side quote away from the mid and about a quarter of that distance is back before the next trade: 24.6% of the distance consumed is replaced on a one-sided surge and 23.8% in a matched quiet window. The share replaced rises with the size of the print, from 0.07 on the smallest tenth of prints inside an episode to 0.40 on the largest tenth. The quote still ends further out after a large print, by a net 2.68 bps at the top decile against 0.09 bps back inside at the bottom decile, and the best level standing at the next trade holds 0.894 of the size that stood before the print, against 0.997 at the bottom decile.

Setup: the three quote readings, the population, and the tick parts

One tick is one fill timestamp inside the surge window. On the side the surge hits, with m the ts_bookdiff_lt mid at that timestamp and s = +1 when the surge side is the ask and -1 when it is the bid, so that away from the mid is positive:

name what it is where it is read
a0_pre the best quote on the surge side just before the taker print at t_i ts_bookdiff_lt at t_i
a0_post the best quote just after that print ts_bookdiff_le at t_i
a1_pre the best quote just before the next trade ts_bookdiff_lt at t_{i+1}, the next fill timestamp of any wallet
q(a0_pre), q(a1_pre) the resting size at the best level in those two states, in HYPE bid_0_amount or ask_0_amount of the same rows

Population. The F1 one-sided surges of tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv and the matched quiet windows of tables/redef2_pop_control_windows.csv, every date. A tick enters the sample when a taker execution consumed the surge side at t_i, which is tk_hype > 0 in the tick parts. Ticks are kept only inside the EVENT phase, t_s to t_e of the surge catalogue and the equivalent window of a control.

Grain. Fill grain only. At book-event grain a1_pre equals a0_post by construction, because the row after le(t_i) is the same book state: measured here, the gap is non-zero on 0.119% of book-grain ticks. The gap carries information only when consecutive rows are further apart than one book event, which at fill grain means the next fill timestamp of any wallet.

Scope. data/tick0922_parts, the side-corrected build of section 68. 1,071,010 surge-side taker ticks on 910 surges over 351 dates, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29, and 808,261 ticks on 558 controls over 276 dates, 2025-03-31 to 2026-06-30. The surge catalogue holds three windows starting on 2025-10-10, contributing 19,522 ticks, and three on 2026-01-31, contributing 3,167. The control catalogue holds no window starting on 2025-10-10 and five on 2026-01-31, contributing 7,598 ticks. The 12 surges absent from the sample are the zero-length entries of the catalogue, which have no surge window.

Compute. code/tickq0922_decile_gaps.py, one pass over the fill-grain tick parts with an 8-worker pool on one soal node, under 2 minutes wall and about 3 GB peak memory. The figure is built by code/tickq0922_figure.py.

69.1 Definitions

Three distances in basis points, measured on the surge side at the fill timestamp t_i:

consumed      c = 1e4 * s * (a0_post - a0_pre) / m
replenished   r = 1e4 * s * (a1_pre  - a0_post) / m
net           d = c + r = 1e4 * s * (a1_pre - a0_pre) / m

c > 0 means the print cleared the best level and pushed the quote away from the mid, which happens on 36.3% of surge ticks; c = 0 means the level absorbed the print with the price unchanged, 53.4%; c < 0 means a quote arrived inside the previous best at the same timestamp, 10.3%. r < 0 means the quote came back toward the mid before the next trade, 20.8% of surge ticks, r > 0 means it moved further out, 7.5%, and r = 0 means the best quote stood unchanged between the two trades, 71.7%.

The replenishment ratio, defined on ticks with c > 0, and the depth ratio, the best-level resting size at the next trade over the size before the print:

rho = -r / c                    1 = back at a0_pre before the next trade, 0 = no replacement
phi = q(a1_pre) / q(a0_pre)     1 = the same size is standing

Each tick is ranked into deciles of the surge-side taker dollars executed at that timestamp, tk_usd = tk_hype * m, within its own event, so prints are compared against other prints of the same episode. Decile 1 is the smallest tenth of prints inside the episode and decile 10 the largest. The alternative ranking, pooling every tick of a population before cutting the deciles, is in the same source file under dec_scheme = pooled; it moves the surge medians by at most 0.24 bps on c and 0.012 on phi, both at decile 10, and rho by at most 0.024, at decile 7.

69.2 The decile ladder

Every measure moves with the size of the print, and the top decile is where the moves become large: from decile 1 to decile 10 the consumed distance runs 1.04 bps to 4.25 bps on the surges, the share replaced 0.07 to 0.40, and the depth standing at the next trade 0.997 to 0.894.

69.3 The regression form

The decile ladder describes the sample; a regression of the replacement on the push measures the same relation in one number and carries a standard error. Conditional resiliency is the standard way to ask this question: the dependent variable is how much of the push comes back before the next trade, the regressor is the push itself, and an event fixed effect absorbs everything that makes one episode different from another, so the slope is identified from the variation in print size inside a single episode, with the difference between a calm episode and a violent one held by the fixed effect. Standard errors are clustered by event, which lets the ticks of one episode be arbitrarily correlated, as they are when one maker quotes the same way for the length of a surge.

r_i     = beta  * c_i + alpha_e(i) + u_i        beta  = share of the push replaced
log phi = gamma * c_i + alpha_e(i) + v_i        gamma = depth response, per bp

Column key and source

One row is one specification. y is the dependent variable: r the replacement in basis points, d = c + r the net distance at the next trade, log phi the log depth ratio. The regressor is c in every row. winsor is the treatment of both variables: none uses them as measured, 1/99 pct clips each at its own 1st and 99th percentile within the population, which matters because c reaches 913 bps on the surges and its standard deviation falls from 9.7 to 2.4 bps under the clip. r carries both treatments because they disagree on the surges; d and log phi are quoted on the clipped variables, and their raw rows are in the source file. Every row carries event fixed effects; the same specifications without them are in the source file under fixed_effects = none and move no slope in this table by more than 0.025. slope is the coefficient on c, cluster SE the standard error clustered by event, t the ratio of the two, within R2 the R-squared after the fixed effects. The event-time profile of the same object, the share of the push reverted at fixed horizons in book events and in clock time, is section 64.7. Source tables/tickq0922_regression.csv, rows fixed_effects = event.

69.4 Findings

As expected.

  • The quote replaces about a quarter of what a print takes, and the share rises with the print. Pooling every tick with c > 0, the replacement is 24.6% of the distance consumed on the surges and 23.8% in the matched windows. Ranked inside the episode, the mean ratio runs 0.07 at decile 1 to 0.40 at decile 10 on the surges and 0.06 to 0.36 on the controls (Tables 21 and 22).
  • A bigger print pushes the quote further and leaves it further out at the next trade. The consumed distance runs 1.04 bps at decile 1 to 4.25 bps at decile 10 on the surges, and the net distance at the next trade runs 0.09 bps back inside to 2.68 bps further out. The regression puts the same relation at 0.72 bps of net distance per bp consumed on the surges and 0.80 on the controls (Table 26).
  • The largest prints are the ones that clear the level. The share of ticks where the print left the best price where it was falls from 0.77 at decile 1 to 0.14 at decile 10 on the surges, and from 0.82 to 0.26 on the controls, so most small prints are absorbed inside the standing best level.
  • The best level standing at the next trade is thinner after a bigger print. The depth ratio runs 0.997 at decile 1 to 0.894 at decile 10 on the surges. The mechanism is the level being eaten: on the ticks where the price did not move the ratio falls to 0.597 at decile 10, while on the ticks where it did move the level exposed behind the eaten one holds 1.11 times its size at decile 10 and 5.11 times at decile 1 (Table 23).
  • Bigger prints are followed sooner by the next trade. The median gap to the next fill runs 350 ms at decile 1 to 251 ms at decile 10 on the surges, against 714 ms to 461 ms on the controls, so the surge measurement window is about half the control's throughout, and the whole ladder is measured over a shorter interval on the surges.
  • Liquidation cascades push hardest per print at the top deciles. At deciles 8 to 10 the consumed distance is 2.69 bps in a cascade and 2.47 bps on a big price move, against 2.14 bps with no big price move, on 46, 312 and 552 events (Table 24).

Not as expected (possible design cause).

  • The raw and the clipped slope disagree on the surges, -0.036 with a clustered standard error of 0.028 against -0.187 with 0.017, while on the controls they bracket each other at -0.264 and -0.191. Possible design cause: 1,465 surge ticks on 140 events carry c above 50 bps, up to 913 bps on 2025-10-10 at 21:17:41, and those pushes are followed by almost no replacement before the next trade, which a level-on-level ordinary least squares reads as a flatter slope. The clipped row is the one to quote; both are kept.
  • The surge and the control replace the same share of a push, -0.187 against -0.191 on all sample ticks and -0.228 against -0.264 on the ticks with c > 0, so the quote comes back at the same rate per basis point pushed in both populations. Possible design cause: the two populations are measured over different windows, a median 290 ms to the next trade on a surge against 616 ms in a control, so the control has twice as long to replace the same push. Check: recompute both at a fixed clock horizon, which section 64.7 already does in event time and clock time for the push-reversion share.
  • The replacement share falls with the push on the surges and rises on the controls at the top of the range. Above 10 bps the aggregate replacement is 0.213 on the surges and 0.417 on the controls, against 0.379 and 0.251 at or below 1 bp (Table 25). Possible design cause: a push above 10 bps in a quiet window is usually one wide tick that a maker steps back into, while the same push inside a surge is a sweep through several levels that nobody refills before the next print arrives 250 ms later. Check: split the above-10-bps bucket by the taker's n_levels and by whether the surge-side quote already stood more than one tick from the mid.
  • Conditional on the print moving the quote, a bigger move goes with a slightly thinner replacement level, -0.008 in log depth per bp with a clustered standard error of 0.003 on the surges and -0.015 with 0.005 on the controls, against +0.110 and +0.271 on the full sample. Possible design cause: phi mixes two states, and the positive full-sample slope is the mix moving from the c = 0 state, where phi sits below 1, toward the c > 0 state, where it sits above 1. Inside the c > 0 state the remaining variation is which level was sitting behind the one eaten, and the relation is measurable but small: a 5 bp push goes with a level 4% thinner.
  • The depth ratio at c > 0 falls from decile 1 to decile 10 here, while section 64.5 reports it falling to a basin over deciles 4 to 8 and rising again to decile 10. Possible design cause: the two are different measurements. That section is at book-event grain on the big-price-move class, ranks on executed size including maker fills, and keeps only ticks the print pushed; this table is at fill grain, ranks on taker dollars, and keeps every surge-side taker tick.

69.5 Validation

Every check in tables/tickq0922_validation.csv passes
  • Per decile the tick counts sum to the population total, 1,071,010 on the surges and 808,261 on the controls, under both ranking schemes, and the ten decile rows of each table sum to its all-decile row.
  • Deciles are balanced inside an event: across the 902 surges with at least 50 sample ticks, the median share of an event's ticks falling in a decile runs 0.0996 to 0.1004 over the ten deciles, and the same range holds across the 558 controls.
  • d equals c + r on all 1,879,271 ticks to 0, and the shares of ticks with c > 0, c = 0 and c < 0 sum to 1 on every tick.
  • Rerunning the tick0922_by_decile recipe on these parts, with its own filters and its own ranking on executed size, reproduces all 480 of its grain = fill rows with a largest absolute difference of 9.1e-13. The sample here is larger, 1,071,010 against 392,705 surge ticks, because this build keeps every surge-side taker tick including the ones where the price did not move.
  • Every date the catalogues reach is present, 351 dates on the surges and 276 on the controls, including 2025-10-10 with 19,522 surge ticks from three windows and 2026-01-31 with 3,167 from three. The control catalogue holds no window starting on 2025-10-10 and five on 2026-01-31, which contribute 7,598 ticks.
  • At book-event grain the gap a1_pre - a0_post is non-zero on 0.119% of the 439,869 surge-side taker ticks, confirming that it is zero by construction at that grain.
  • Dropping the 2025-03-24 to 2025-05-25 dates, where the maker and taker fill rows do not balance, moves the surge ratio from 0.301 to 0.298 on 801 events and the control ratio from 0.211 to 0.214 on 491. Those dates hold 7.0% of the surge ticks and 6.2% of the control ticks.
  • Ticks where only a maker fill row exists on the surge side, 1.1% on the surges and 1.8% on the controls, sit outside the sample, which requires a taker execution.

69.6 What this does not establish

  • "The next trade" is the next fill timestamp of any wallet, not the next print on the surge side. The replacement window is a median 290 ms on a surge and 616 ms in a control, so the two populations are compared over windows of different length, and the surge-minus-control comparisons in Table 26 carry that difference inside them.
  • The gap is identically zero at book-event grain, so nothing here reads as a statement about what happens between two consecutive book events. It is a statement about what happens between two trades.
  • r mixes new quotes with cancels. A value of r < 0 means the best quote ended nearer the mid than a0_post, which a placement inside and a cancel further out both produce; nothing here attributes the replacement to any wallet or to the market makers specifically. Attribution needs the order store, which the tick build does not read.
  • The deciles are a ranking, not a treatment. A tick lands in decile 10 because the taker chose to send a large order at that moment, which is also when the book was thin or the price was moving, so the ladder describes what follows a large print, and the causal reading stays open.
  • The event fixed effect absorbs the episode, not the minute. Within one surge the early and late minutes differ in depth and in spread, and the slope pools them.

70. What separates the surges whose price reverts from those that hold

Whether the price of a one-sided taker surge is still standing 15 minutes later is decided by the taker flow that arrives after the run ends: the median event that holds takes another $0.43m of net taker volume in the surge direction over those 15 minutes, and the median event that reverts meets $3.16m of net taker volume against it. The surge-side quote says the same over the same 15 minutes, traveling 0.97, 1.04 and 1.10 bps back toward the mid for every 1 bps away across the events that hold, the partly reverted and the reverted. Everything measured while the run is under way reads the same across the three patterns: the market-maker population's quote tilt, the execution and cancel shares of the quote's travel, the surge-side depth and the size of the surge itself.

Setup: population, grain, windows, sources

One row is one event. The population is the 922 F1 one-sided taker surges of tables/redef4_price_class.csv (family == 'F1'), carrying the price pattern of record from section 41.4 of analysis.md: 206 held, 224 partly reverted, 62 reverted (492 gated events), 428 flat and 2 against. The flat events are a reference column throughout; the 2 against events are counted in validation and not tabulated.

Every date in the sample is included, 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31 among them, 351 dates with three events on each of those two. The gated runs last 15 minutes at the median (p5 5, p25 11, p75 25, p95 42).

Sources, all experiment-local: the price pattern, anchors and peak move from tables/redef4_price_class.csv and tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv; taker flow in 1-minute bins from data/market_taker_1m.parquet; the market-maker population from tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv, rows with shocked_loose == True, the accumulating population of section 64.3; quote travel at the book from surge-side fill-grain ticks rebuilt by code/rev0922_reverted_vs_held.py --stage ticks into data/rev0922_tick_parts/, from the same inputs as the fill-grain build; spread and depth by phase from tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_event.csv.

The surge side is rebuilt here, on the side the takers consumed, ask for a buy surge and bid for a sell surge, which is the defect and the fix of section 68. Validation reproduces the published tick0921 numbers exactly on the 476 sell surges that carry a run-phase unit.

Builder code/rev0922_reverted_vs_held.py, run 2026-09-22. Tables tables/rev0922_by_pattern.csv, _spearman.csv, _ols.csv, _excursion_baselines.csv, _cascade_top10.csv, _validation.csv and the per-event feature table _event_features.csv.

70.1 Definitions

The outcome. rho_15 = M_final(15) / M_peak, the share of the peak move still standing 15 minutes after the run ends, both moves in the surge direction and anchored on p_start, the mid at the run's first minute t_s. The pattern of record splits the gated events at rho_15 >= 0.75 (held), 0.25 <= rho_15 < 0.75 (partly reverted) and rho_15 < 0.25 (reverted). An event is gated when its peak move clears g, the full-sample p95 of the 1-minute peak move for its length class.

The run window and the window after it. The run is the minutes [t_s, t_e] inclusive, which reproduces the catalogue's own length_min_1m on all 922 events. The window after the run is the 15 minutes (t_e, t_e + 15 min], the same look-ahead that rho_15 uses.

Taker flow. With d = +1 on a buy surge and d = -1 on a sell surge, the surge-side USD is the taker volume on side d inside the run and the opposite-side USD is the taker volume on side -d. The flow after the run is

net_post = d * (taker buy USD - taker sell USD)   over (t_e, t_e + 15 min]

so positive means the flow keeps pushing the price the way the surge pushed it. The forced share is liquidation taker USD over all taker USD inside the run.

Market-maker tilt. tilt_bps = d(SAME) - d(OPP) against the same market maker's own PRE2H value, in that market maker's own ACC and UNW windows as Table 3 defines them, positive when the exit quote sits nearer the touch. The event's value is the median across its accumulating market makers. The two side distances are reported separately, each as d(side, phase) - d(side, PRE2H), positive when that side's best quote moved away from the mid. The exit-side size share is size(OPP) / (size(OPP) + size(SAME)).

Quote travel at the book. On the surge side, at every timestamp t_i at which a fill occurred, with m_i the pre-event mid and s = +1 on the ask, -1 on the bid,

c_bps      = 1e4 * s * (le(t_i)     - lt(t_i))  / m_i   what the fills and cancels did
r_bps      = 1e4 * s * (lt(t_{i+1}) - le(t_i))  / m_i   what happened before the next fill
away_total = sum(c_bps > 0) + sum(r_bps > 0)            gross travel away from the mid

away_total splits into trade, mixed, cancel at a fill and between fills by the fill-grain rule of section 64.6, and the execution share is the trade part over away_total. The mirror quantity is the gross travel back toward the mid, the negative parts of the same two terms, and the ratio of the two is above 1 when the quote ends the window nearer the mid than it started. The share of an executed push undone at 5 s and 30 s is 1 - (quote at the horizon - quote before the push) / c_bps, median over the run's executed pushes; a negative value means the quote kept traveling away.

Spread and depth. PEAK_c is the 3 minutes [t_c - 1 min, t_c + 2 min) and PRE2H the 2 hours before t_s. The peak-minute spread ratio is mean spread in PEAK_c over mean spread in PRE2H; the depth ratio is the median resting size within 10 bps of the mid over the same two windows.

Sign convention and the two tests. Every signed separator is named for the direction it measures and carries the sign its mechanism predicts for the Spearman against rho_15 (expected_sign_vs_rho15 in tables/rev0922_spearman.csv). The oriented Spearman, rho_oriented = rho * expected_sign, is positive when the mechanism holds. Measures with no directional prediction carry sign 0 and no oriented value. The Kruskal-Wallis H test asks whether the three gated patterns draw their values of a separator from the same distribution, using ranks only. The Spearman rho is the correlation of the ranks of a separator with the ranks of rho_15 across the 492 gated events. Because 32 separators are tested, the Bonferroni threshold is 0.05 / 32 = 0.0016.

Figure 7. Nine candidate separators by price pattern.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

One panel per separator, dot at the median and bar from p25 to p75 over the events of that pattern; each panel carries its own event count because the market-maker and book measures are missing on some events. The flat events are the reference column and are excluded from every rank test. Panel 1 is the surge's size, panels 2 and 3 the flow and the quote over the 15 minutes after the run, panels 4 and 5 the population's quote tilt in its two phases, panels 6 and 7 the book decomposition inside the run, and panels 8 and 9 the spread and depth at the pressure peak, each against the event's own prior 2 hours. The horizontal rule is 0 where a measure is signed and 1 where it is a ratio.

70.2 Taker flow

The size of the surge separates the gated events from the flat ones and says nothing about which gated events revert: the median surge-side volume is $15.0m on the events that hold, $17.6m on the partly reverted, $15.2m on the events that revert and $8.5m on the flat events. The events that revert are the ones the flow turns against afterwards, meeting 0.23 of the run's own volume in the opposite direction over the next 15 minutes, against 0.03 more in the surge direction on the events that hold.

70.3 The market-maker population

The population repeats the shape of section 64.3 on every pattern: the quote leans away from the exit while the position builds and turns back toward it during the unwind, with the absorption side carrying the turn. The unwind tilt is +1.09 bps on the events that hold, +1.46 on the partly reverted and +0.74 on the events that revert, a 0.72 bps spread on a distribution whose interquartile range is 5.7 bps, and the rank test puts the three patterns at p = 0.90. The accumulation tilt orders with the outcome, at -13.6, -15.0 and -18.0 bps, and its rank test is p = 0.060, above the 0.0016 threshold that 32 tests require.

70.4 Quote travel at the book

Executions move about three quarters of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid in every pattern, 0.756 on the events that hold, 0.778 on the partly reverted and 0.784 on the events that revert, and cancels move 4% in all three. The book measure that orders with the outcome sits after the run and is the price path read off the quote: over the 15 minutes after t_e the surge-side quote travels 0.968 bps back toward the mid for every 1 bps away on the events that hold, 1.041 on the partly reverted and 1.101 on the events that revert, on 492 events with no missing value, and both directions carry more travel on the events that revert, 1,437 bps away against 1,168.

70.9 Findings

As expected.

  • The flow after the run separates the patterns and nothing measured inside the run does. The median event that holds takes another $0.43m of net taker volume in the surge direction over the 15 minutes after t_e, and the median event that reverts meets $3.16m of net taker volume against it, which as a fraction of the run's own surge-side volume is +0.03 against -0.23. The rank test is H = 129.7 at p = 6.7e-29 on 492 events and the Spearman against rho_15 is +0.56.
  • The size of the surge separates gated from flat and says nothing about reversion. The median surge-side volume is $15.0m on the events that hold, $17.6m on the partly reverted, $15.2m on the reverted and $8.5m on the flat, with a rank test of p = 0.29 across the three gated patterns.
  • The population's unwind tilt is the same on every pattern. +1.09 bps on the events that hold, +1.46 partly reverted, +0.74 reverted, against an interquartile range of 5.7 bps and a rank test of p = 0.90 on 442 events. The +1.55 bps of section 64.3 holds across all of them.
  • Executions move about three quarters of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid in every pattern, 0.756 held and 0.784 reverted (p = 0.28), and cancels move 4% in every pattern (p = 0.82). The execution share of section 64.6 does not depend on what the price does afterwards.
  • The surge-side quote ends the 15 minutes after the run nearer the mid on the events that revert. Travel back toward the mid over travel away is 0.968 on the events that hold, 1.041 partly reverted and 1.101 reverted, H = 216.0 at p = 1.2e-47 on 492 events, the strongest ordering of any separator here. Both directions carry more travel on the events that revert, 1,437 bps away against 1,168.
  • Only the flow after the run survives the multivariate fit. In the standardized ordinary least squares of rho_15, the flow after the run carries +0.113 per standard deviation with an HC3 standard error of 0.032, and the other five terms are within 1.0 standard error of zero. R-squared is 0.149 on 439 events.
  • A longer baseline makes every peak move larger and the retention ratio higher, and the classification mostly survives it: the median gated peak move is 260 bps on the t_s mid and 410 bps on the 12-hour median mid, and 384 of 492 gated events keep their pattern when rho_15 is re-anchored on the 2-hour median mid.

Not as expected (possible design cause).

  • The accumulation tilt is largest on the events that revert, which is the opposite of the mechanism. The tilt against the market maker's own prior 2 hours is -13.6 bps on the events that hold and -18.0 on the events that revert, so the population quotes further away from the exit on the events whose price comes back. Possible design cause: the tilt is a minute-snapshot measure of where orders were resting, and a reverting event is the one where the price ran furthest fastest, which drags a stale resting order's distance to the mid without the market maker having moved it. Check: recompute the tilt at the order's own placement time when the placement-time build lands, on the same 492 events, and compare the pattern ordering. This is decision D9 of section 64.11.
  • The reverted events draw fewer accumulating market makers and a smaller share of the surge. 5 accumulating market makers at the median against 7 on the events that hold, absorbing 7.2% of the surge's taker USD against 13.5%. Possible design cause: the reverted events are the shortest and fastest, 9.5 minutes from t_s to the price extreme against 25 on the events that hold, and the population rule needs an inventory excursion measured over minutes to flag a market maker at all. Check: recompute the population share on a duration-matched subsample, or per minute of run length.
  • The time from the run's start to the price extreme orders with the pattern as strongly as the flow does, 25 minutes held, 16.5 partly reverted and 9.5 reverted, H = 95.7 at p = 1.7e-21. This is a property of the outcome window: the peak and the 15-minute endpoint are both searched inside the same look-ahead, so an event whose extreme arrives early has more of the window left in which to lose the move. Check: recompute rho_15 on a fixed 30-minute horizon from t_pp in place of t_e and see whether the ordering survives.

70.10 Validation

Every check in tables/rev0922_validation.csv passes unless noted
  • 922 events = 492 gated + 428 flat + 2 against, and the gated split reproduces section 41.4 of analysis.md exactly: 206 held, 224 partly reverted, 62 reverted. The gated flag equals big_move_full on every event.
  • All 351 dates are kept, with three events on 2025-10-10 and three on 2026-01-31.
  • The surge-side taker USD computed here reproduces the catalogue's own hit_usd_1m to 2.3e-16 relative on all 922 events, and the run's minute count equals length_min_1m on all 922.
  • The rebuilt ticks reproduce tables/tick0921_event_decomp.csv share_trade to 1.1e-16 on the 476 sell surges that carry a run-phase unit, which is the subset where the published build happened to measure the surge side. On the 434 buy surges with a unit the two differ by a median 0.082.
  • The four travel shares sum to 1 on all 910 events with travel in the run, to 2.2e-16.
  • Coverage on the 492 gated events, stated per separator in the validation table: flow and the peak-excursion measures 492 of 492; the book measures 490 in the run, because two events have t_e equal to t_s, and 492 after it; spread and depth 490; the market-maker measures 433 to 478, the shortfall being 14 gated events with no accumulating market maker and a further 25 to 45 whose market makers lack a resting order on one side in the accumulation or the unwind window. No event is dropped silently: every quantile cell in every table carries its own n.
  • The accumulating population is 6,173 of the 118,269 (event, market maker) rows of tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv, spread over 849 of the 922 events, the same cut that section 64.3 reports. Resting size is zero on both sides in the PRE2H window on 8.2% of those rows, the order-store defect of decision D3, which is why the exit-side size share carries a smaller n than the distances.

70.11 What this does not establish

  • rho_15 is a 15-minute look-ahead, and the three strongest separators are measured over the same 15 minutes. The net taker flow after the run and the price path it is compared against occupy the same window, so the two move together by construction as much as by mechanism, and nothing here says the flow arrived first. The quote's travel back over its travel away is stronger still and carries less information: it is read off the same best-quote series whose midpoint defines rho_15, so it restates the outcome in book units. The minutes from t_s to the price extreme are a property of the same window.
  • The tilt is a minute-snapshot measure. q_ACC_* and q_UNW_* read the distance from each resting order to the minute's mid on a 1-minute grid, so they record where orders sat during the minute. The placement-time measure is a different object, and the accumulation-tilt finding above is the one most likely to move under it.
  • With 32 separators tested, 4 clear the Bonferroni threshold of 0.0016: the two flow measures after the run, the quote's back-over-away ratio after the run and the time to the price extreme. The spread ratio at 0.054, the accumulation tilt at 0.060 and the market-maker count at 0.055 are readings a single pre-registered test would have called, and no test here was pre-registered.
  • The ordinary least squares is descriptive. Its terms are contemporaneous with each other and with the outcome, the dollar terms are right-skewed and standardizing them does not fix that, and 53 of the 492 gated events are dropped for a missing input. No coefficient identifies an effect.
  • The book measures cover the surge side only. The opposite side's quote travel is not measured here, so the section cannot say whether the far side's quotes moved differently on the events that revert; the other-side depth ratio of Table 30 is a 1-minute resting-size measure, not a tick measure.
  • ts_bookdiff_lt and _le are a reconstruction whose timestamp tie-break is not HyperCore's documented action ordering, and a tick carrying a fill and a placement at the same microsecond cannot be split, so the trade and cancel attribution is a lower bound on how mixed the ticks are.

71. Liquidation cascades as time episodes

HYPE has 301 liquidation episodes above $1m of liquidated notional over 2025-04-01 to 2026-06-30, and 187 of them, 62.1%, share at least one minute with an event in the one-sided surge catalogue or the net-flow box catalogue. That clears the coverage rule's 60% bar, so at the 15-minute gap rule the flow catalogues reach most cascades. They clear it narrowly and only from 15 minutes upward: under a 5-minute gap the share is 57.1%. Coverage is much stronger in dollars than in episodes, because the caught episodes are the large ones: they hold $1,383.7m of the $1,624.4m that the 301 episodes liquidate, 85.2%. In the other direction the two definitions agree completely at the top: all 47 one-sided surges labeled a liquidation cascade contain an episode, and 45 of them contain one above the $1m floor.

Setup: populations, sources and compute

The liquidation stream. Every HYPE trade in data_enriched/hype/grouped_trade_oid/{date}.parquet with dir_bucket == 'liquidation', over the 456 daily partitions from 2025-04-01 to 2026-06-30: 101,590 trades, $1,965.2m of liquidated notional, 48,961 distinct victim wallets, on 435 of the 456 dates. dir_bucket is assigned in the priority adl > liquidation > open > reversal > close, and liquidated_volume > 0 is set only where the fill's liquidatedUser == user, so this bucket is exactly the victim side of a liquidation that was not auto-deleveraged. The 6,230 ADL trades on the same dates, $189.9m, are excluded, as docs/conventions.md requires. Both maker and taker roles are kept: 21.1% of the liquidated notional fills maker-side, so a crossed == true filter would drop a fifth of the stream and drop it unevenly across episodes.

The flow catalogues. The 922 one-sided taker surges, tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv, windows t_s_utc to t_e_utc. The 915 net-flow boxes, tables/redef2_imb_events_recommended_absgate.csv, windows start_utc to end_utc. Four one-sided surges fall on 2025-03-30 and 2025-03-31, before the episode window opens; three carry the no-big-price-move class and one the big-price-move class.

Reused. The extraction contract, meaning the source table, the column list and the victim definition, comes from Allium/experiments/leverage/code/build_liq_trades_sidecar.py. The gap-run episode labeling comes from Allium/experiments/leverage/leverage_cohort/wrapup_2026-09-06/code/build_cascade_episodes.py, with its per-coin partition dropped because this stream is one coin. The Allium sidecar file itself starts on 2025-09-27 and covers only the last nine months of this window, so the extraction is rerun on HYPE alone against the same source partitions.

Builder. code/casc0922_episodes.py, run 2026-09-22 inside the interactive allocation, 16 reader threads, 16 seconds wall. Outputs tables/casc0922_episodes.csv, _summary.csv, _top10.csv, _overlap_f1.csv, _f1_by_class.csv, _caught_vs_missed.csv, _monthly.csv and figures/redefinition/casc0922_episodes_timeline.png.

Every exhibit includes 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31. No date is excluded anywhere in this section.

71.1 Two definitions of a cascade, side by side

The project uses the word cascade for two different objects: a class label on an event a flow rule already selected, and a run of liquidation trades that is an event in its own right.

The class label. A property of an event that is already in a flow catalogue. An event is labeled a liquidation cascade when forced taker USD inside its window is at least a tenth of all taker USD in that window:

forced_share = (liquidation USD + ADL USD taken inside the window) / taker USD inside the window
liq_cascade  = forced_share >= 0.10

It holds for 47 of the 922 one-sided surges and 41 of the 915 net-flow boxes. It can only label surges the flow rules already selected.

The time episode. An event in its own right, selected on liquidations. Order the victim-side HYPE liquidation trades by timestamp and cut the sequence wherever consecutive trades sit more than g minutes apart. Each maximal run is one episode:

episode boundary at trade i  <=>  t(i) - t(i-1) > g minutes
g = 15 minutes for the headline, with g = 5, 30 and 60 as sensitivity

Per episode the quantities are the first and last liquidation timestamp, the elapsed minutes between them, the summed liquidated notional and HYPE size, the count of distinct victim wallets, the count of liquidation trades, and the dominant side, which is forced_sell when victims with long positions supply the larger share of the liquidated notional and forced_buy otherwise.

The floor. An episode enters the coverage population when its liquidated notional is at least $1m, the level Xinmeng fixed on 2026-09-21. At the 15-minute gap the floor keeps 301 of 4,159 episodes and 82.7% of the liquidated notional; the median episode below it liquidates $10.9k across three wallets.

Overlap. An episode and a flow event overlap when their closed minute intervals share a minute. Both catalogues store an inclusive last minute, so the event interval is [t_s, t_e] for a one-sided surge and [start_utc, end_utc] for a net-flow box, and the episode interval is the first and last liquidation minute. gap_to_nearest_flow_min is the minute distance from an episode to the closest event of either catalogue and is 0 where they overlap. Overlap is a timing statement and carries no claim that the liquidations caused the surge.

71.2 How many episodes there are, and how many the catalogues reach

The $1m floor decides which liquidation runs count as cascades and the gap rule barely moves that set: the episode count falls from 6,316 at a 5-minute gap to 2,104 at 60 minutes while the count above the floor stays between 262 and 301. Coverage of the above-floor episodes rises with the gap, from 57.1% at 5 minutes to 81.3% at 60.

Column key and source

One row per gap rule and floor. episodes is the count of maximal runs; notional is their summed liquidated notional in millions of dollars, which equals the whole stream at every gap when no floor applies; duration and victims are medians across episodes, in minutes and distinct wallets.   • The floor decides which episodes are cascades, and the gap rule barely moves that set. The episode count falls from 6,316 at the 5-minute gap to 2,104 at 60, while the count above the $1m floor stays between 262 and 301. Runs that merge under a wider gap were already large enough to clear the floor separately.
  • Coverage rises with the gap, and the verdict turns on it. The share of above-floor episodes overlapping a flow event runs 57.1%, 62.1%, 69.9% and 81.3% across the four gap rules, so the 60% bar is met at 15, 30 and 60 minutes and missed at 5.
  • Dollar coverage is 23 points higher than episode coverage. At the 15-minute gap the caught episodes are 62.1% of the count and 85.2% of the notional, so the episodes the catalogues reach are the large ones.
  • Both catalogues are needed and the surge catalogue does most of the work. Of the 301 above-floor episodes, 86 overlap both catalogues, 86 a one-sided surge alone, 15 a net-flow box alone and 114 neither. The 86 that overlap both hold $1,100.9m, two thirds of the population's notional.

The 10% forced-share label separates the classes the way it is meant to: 9.1% of the quiet surges hold an episode above the $1m floor against 25.5% of the big-price-move class and 95.7% of the events the label calls a liquidation cascade.

One row per class3_abs class of the one-sided surge catalogue.
